catalog_locator: sec. 2.3 'Length and stress', pp. 41-42 (PDF pp. 9-10 of)
catalog_quote: There is a close relationship between vowel length and stress. In a word of two syllables, in which neither vowel is long, stress ordinarily falls on the first syllable, e.g.: námbal 'stone'. A word with more than two syllables, again without long vowels, has primary stress on the first syllable, and secondary stress on all odd numbered syllables, e.g.: márrbugàn 'cave', bígibìgi 'pig' ... Long vowels always bear stress. ... Words with long first syllables and with short vowels in the remaining syllables follow the same stress pattern as words with no long vowels ... When a disyllabic word has a short first vowel and a long second vowel, the first syllable is unstressed and the second stressed: magíil 'branch' gabíirr 'girl' If both syllables are long, both receive equal (or near equal) stress: búurráay 'water' ngáanáa 'what' Long vowels are not found after the second syllable of a word…

sources.note: The source the StressTyp2 entry for this language cites for 'initial primary, trochaic secondary'; our record carries an unresolved 'agrees only in part / not reachable' contra note against it. Reading p. 29 would show whether de Zwaan simply omits the short+long disyllable case (magíil) that makes Haviland's description weight-sensitive, closing the StressTyp2 discrepancy. Would not change the classification (Haviland 1979 supersedes it).
